Will the CDU and Greens remain fragmented enough in voter support that AfD can finish first with only a plurality in the low-to-mid 20s or similar range?
A) Yes. Mainstream competition will stay divided enough that AfD can come first without needing an exceptionally high vote share.
B) No. At least one major mainstream party—most likely CDU or Greens—will consolidate enough support to stay ahead of AfD.

Will AfD’s support in Baden-Württemberg prove robust through election day rather than slipping because of campaign effects, scandals, mobilization against it, or tactical voting?
A) Yes. AfD’s support will hold steady through election day, with little late-campaign erosion.
B) No. AfD will lose some support before election day because of backlash, turnout differentials, or strategic consolidation against it.

Will AfD's vote share in Baden-Württemberg hold up through election day rather than falling relative to late polls?
A) AfD's supporters are motivated and its final result will match or exceed late polling rather than softening.
B) AfD will underperform late polls because of tactical voting, late undecideds breaking away, or turnout/composition effects.

By the final stretch of the Baden-Württemberg campaign, will AfD be polling at or above the leading mainstream party in statewide vote intention?
A) Yes. AfD will be at or near first place in late polling, showing it has a realistic path to top seat count.
B) No. AfD will remain behind at least one mainstream party in late polling, implying it is still an underdog for most seats.

Will AfD be polling within realistic striking distance of first place in Baden-Württemberg during the final pre-election stretch?
A) Yes. Late-cycle polling will show AfD close enough to the top that ordinary campaign volatility could put it in first place.
B) No. Final pre-election polling will show AfD clearly behind the top party or parties, outside normal error from first place.

Will fragmentation among CDU, Greens, SPD, FDP, Left/BSW/others make it possible to win first place with a relatively low plurality vote share?
A) Yes. The party system will remain fragmented enough that first place may require only a modest plurality in the high-20s or even lower.
B) No. Fragmentation will not be extreme enough, or will diminish late in the race, so the winning party will need a stronger vote share that AfD is unlikely to reach.

Will AfD be within realistic striking distance of first place in Baden-Württemberg state polling during the final pre-election period, rather than remaining clearly behind both Greens and CDU?
A) AfD will be polling close enough to first place near the election that a first-place finish is a live outcome.
B) AfD will still be clearly behind at least one major rival in late polling, making first place unlikely.

Will there be a major late-campaign shock or national-political development that materially boosts AfD relative to the Greens and CDU in Baden-Württemberg?
A) Yes. The seat allocation and district/list dynamics will not meaningfully disadvantage AfD relative to its vote share; if it tops votes, it likely tops seats.
B) No. There will be no major late event that significantly improves AfD’s standing beyond baseline trends.

Are recent Baden-Württemberg state-level polls showing AfD genuinely competitive for first place in vote share, rather than clearly behind the Greens or CDU?
A) Yes. Multiple recent, credible Baden-Württemberg polls place AfD at or near first, within a margin where first place is a live possibility.
B) No. Reliable Baden-Württemberg polling still shows AfD clearly behind at least one major rival, making first place unlikely absent a late shock.

Will Baden-Württemberg vote substantially more anti-AfD than Germany as a whole at the time of the election?
A) Baden-Württemberg will not vote substantially more anti-AfD than Germany as a whole at the time of the election.
B) Baden-Württemberg will vote substantially more anti-AfD than Germany as a whole at the time of the election.

Will AfD's Baden-Württemberg vote share by election day be high enough to reach the upper-20s or better, making first place realistically attainable?
A) AfD's vote share in Baden-Württemberg will rise into a range where first place is realistically attainable.
B) AfD's vote share in Baden-Württemberg will stay below the range usually needed for first place.

Will national political deterioration for mainstream parties persist through the election rather than partially reversing before voters cast ballots?
A) Yes. Mainstream governing parties will still be suffering from national dissatisfaction by election time, with no strong recovery in credibility, economic conditions, or migration management.
B) No. National conditions may improve somewhat or voter anger may diffuse, allowing mainstream parties to recover enough ground before the election to keep AfD from finishing first.

Will either CDU or Greens consolidate enough anti-AfD and mainstream support to clearly outpoll AfD?
A) No. Neither CDU nor Greens will consolidate enough support to open a clear lead over AfD.
B) Yes. CDU or Greens will consolidate mainstream voters and remain clearly ahead of AfD.

Will AfD avoid a meaningful late-campaign decline caused by mobilization against it, scandal, or strategic voting?
A) Yes. AfD will hold its support through the campaign without a major late drop.
B) No. AfD will suffer a notable late-campaign erosion from counter-mobilization, scandal, or strategic voting.

Will anti-AfD tactical voting and strategic coordination among voters be weak enough that AfD can win a plurality, rather than strong enough to block it?
A) Yes. Many anti-AfD voters stay with their preferred parties instead of coordinating behind the strongest blocker.
B) No. Strategic anti-AfD voting is strong enough to concentrate support on the most viable rival.

Will AfD avoid major state-level scandals, candidate problems, or mobilization backlash that would materially depress its vote share?
A) Yes. AfD runs a sufficiently disciplined campaign without major shocks that would scare off wavering voters.
B) No. Candidate controversies, extremist associations, or anti-AfD tactical mobilization materially weaken its result.

Will AfD be polling at or near first place in Baden-Württemberg close to election day?
A) Yes. Late-state polling shows AfD roughly tied for first or clearly competitive for first.
B) No. Late polling has AfD clearly behind at least one of CDU or Greens.

Is there a realistic path for major campaign events before the election to shift the issue agenda toward topics that empirically benefit AfD more than its rivals?
A) Yes. Plausible events or issue salience shifts could objectively increase the weight of topics on which AfD tends to gain support.
B) No. Absent an unusually large shock, the issue environment is unlikely to change enough to significantly improve AfD's position relative to competitors.

Will anti-incumbent and migration-focused voter sentiment remain strong enough in the state to drive an AfD plurality surge?
A) Yes. Migration, economic frustration, and anti-establishment sentiment will be sufficiently intense to lift AfD above the mainstream parties.
B) No. Issue salience may help AfD somewhat, but not enough to overcome the state’s baseline preference for established parties.

Will mainstream governing parties at federal and state levels remain sufficiently unpopular that anti-incumbent sentiment benefits AfD, rather than incumbents or established opposition recovering by election time?
A) Yes. Dissatisfaction with mainstream parties remains high or worsens, and AfD captures the protest vote.
B) No. Mainstream parties recover some credibility or channel discontent better than expected, blunting AfD’s gains.

Will one major mainstream party in Baden-Württemberg consolidate enough support to stay clearly ahead of AfD, rather than the mainstream vote remaining fragmented?
A) No. The mainstream field will stay fragmented, with Greens, CDU, SPD, FDP, and others dividing the non-AfD electorate enough that AfD can come first with a plurality rather than a majority.
B) Yes. Either the Greens or CDU will consolidate enough support to remain the clear leading party, preventing AfD from benefiting from opposition fragmentation.

Will late tactical or strategic voting among anti-AfD voters significantly reduce AfD’s chance of finishing first?
A) Yes. Voters who primarily want to block AfD will coalesce late behind the strongest rival, hurting AfD’s finishing position.
B) Yes. Migration, economic stress, security, or anti-incumbent backlash will dominate and play to AfD’s strengths.

Will AfD’s statewide vote share in Baden-Württemberg rise enough by election day to place it at or near first place in votes, rather than remaining clearly behind the Greens or CDU?
A) Yes. AfD’s support will continue rising or hold at a high enough level that first place in votes is realistically attainable.
B) No. AfD will improve somewhat or stall, but remain below at least one of the Greens or CDU in statewide vote share.

Will AfD be polling at or above the CDU in Baden-Württemberg during the final month before the election?
A) Yes. AfD will be at or above CDU in late polling, indicating it has a live or leading path to first place.
B) No. CDU will still be clearly ahead in late polling, making AfD first place unlikely.

Will the leading mainstream competitor in Baden-Württemberg remain strong enough that first place requires AfD to exceed its historical state-level ceiling by a substantial margin?
A) No. The leading mainstream party will not be robustly dominant; fragmentation will leave first place attainable on a relatively modest vote share.
B) Yes. At least one mainstream competitor will stay strong enough that AfD would need an unusually high result beyond its plausible state range to finish first.
